raw_findings.message: The gzip command's error is discarded, so if compression fails the CLI still reports success despite not producing the expected compressed output.
The user-controlled `-out` value is concatenated into a shell command, so a value containing shell metacharacters can execute arbitrary commands.
When `-workers` is zero or negative no goroutines consume jobs or send results, so the CLI blocks indefinitely for nonempty input.
Each opened file is deferred until its worker exits rather than closed after parsing, so processing enough input files can exhaust the process's file descriptors.
Multiple workers update the shared `counts` map without synchronization, which can cause a data race or a fatal concurrent-map-write panic.
The timestamp parse error is ignored, so malformed timestamps become zero-time records and are included in summaries when no `-since` filter is set.
Summing parsed latencies can overflow `int64`, causing the reported average to be incorrect for sufficiently large latency values or totals.
If no records are parsed or remain after filtering, dividing by `len(records)` panics instead of producing a summary or returning an error.
Slicing `paths` by the unvalidated `-top` value panics when it is negative or greater than the number of distinct paths.
Percentiles are not range-checked, so values below zero or at least 100 produce an out-of-range index and panic when records are present.

raw_findings.message: The gzip command's error is ignored, so if gzip fails the CLI still reports success even though the requested compression did not occur.
The output path is concatenated into a shell command, so a crafted `--out` value can execute arbitrary commands when `sh -c` runs.
If `--workers` is zero or negative, no goroutine reads from `jobs`, so the producer blocks and the command hangs.
Each opened file is deferred for closing until its worker exits, so processing enough files can exhaust the process's file descriptors before any are closed.
Workers increment the shared `counts` map without synchronization, so concurrent file processing can trigger a data race or fatal concurrent-map-write panic.
A malformed timestamp is silently replaced with the zero time, causing the record to be counted without a filter or incorrectly excluded by a `--since` filter.
Adding valid `int64` latencies can overflow `total`, producing an incorrect average for inputs whose latency sum exceeds the `int64` range.
If no records are parsed or all records are filtered out, `len(records)` is zero and computing the average panics.
Slicing with `top` panics when it is negative or greater than the number of distinct paths, which can occur with the default `--top 5` on a small input.
A percentile outside the supported index range, such as `--percentiles 100` or a negative value, produces an out-of-range index and panics.

exec.Command resolves gzip through PATH, so an attacker who controls PATH can cause the CLI to execute a malicious program instead of gzip.
ParseInt accepts negative latency values, which can make averages and percentiles report impossible negative latencies when an input record contains a negative value.
Adding valid int64 latency values can overflow total and produce an incorrect average, for example when two records contain values near MaxInt64.
An attacker-controlled path is written verbatim into the summary, allowing escape sequences in a log record to manipulate or spoof the terminal when the summary is printed.

fixed_raw_findings.message: `os.WriteFile` follows an existing symlink at the output path, so running the CLI in an attacker-controlled directory can overwrite the symlink target.
The unqualified `gzip` command is resolved through `PATH`, allowing an attacker who controls the process environment to execute a substitute binary.
Negative latency values are accepted as valid, so a log record such as `-5ms` can produce negative averages and percentiles.

A path field from an input log is printed without escaping, so an attacker can include terminal control sequences that execute when the summary is viewed in a terminal.
